---
title: "Structs in Rust"
---


A **struct** is a custom data type that groups related values under one name. If you know C# or Dart, think of a class with only fields. The key difference is that in Rust, **data and behavior are kept apart**:

```
   C# / Dart / Python class            Rust
  ┌─────────────────────────┐    ┌──────────────┐
  │ fields                  │    │ struct       │ ← data only
  │ constructor             │    ├──────────────┤
  │ methods                 │ →  │ impl block   │ ← behavior (methods, constructors)
  │ inheritance (extends)   │    ├──────────────┤
  │ interfaces (implements) │    │ trait impls  │ ← shared behavior (≈ interfaces)
  └─────────────────────────┘    └──────────────┘
                                  No inheritance: composition + traits instead
```

---

## 1. Defining and creating a struct

```rust
struct User {
    username: String,
    email: String,
    active: bool,
    login_count: u64,
}
```

To create an instance, you must give a value for **every** field. Rust has no default `null`:

```rust
let user1 = User {
    username: String::from("lightbridge"),
    email: String::from("lb@example.com"),
    active: true,
    login_count: 0,
};
println!("{}", user1.email); // dot access, as you'd expect
```

**Mutability applies to the whole instance, not to single fields.** Rust has no `mut` on individual fields:

```rust
let mut user2 = User { /* ... */ };
user2.login_count += 1;   // OK, because user2 is `mut`
// user1.active = false;  // ❌ compile error: user1 is immutable
```

**Field init shorthand.** When a variable has the same name as a field, you can write the name once, like JS object shorthand:

```rust
fn build_user(username: String, email: String) -> User {
    User { username, email, active: true, login_count: 0 }
}
```

**Struct update syntax.** This works like JS spread, but with one ownership catch:

```rust
let user3 = User {
    email: String::from("new@example.com"),
    ..user1          // take the remaining fields from user1
};
// ⚠️ user1.username (a String) was MOVED into user3.
// user1 can no longer be used as a whole.
```

The `bool` and `u64` fields are copied, but `String` is moved. This is the first place where structs and ownership meet.

---

## 2. Three kinds of structs

```
┌────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┐
│ Kind               │ Syntax                      │ Typical use                │
├────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────┤
│ Named-field        │ struct User { name: String }│ Most data models           │
│ Tuple struct       │ struct Meters(f64);         │ Newtypes, small groupings  │
│ Unit-like struct   │ struct Marker;              │ Types that carry no data,  │
│                    │                             │ used to implement traits   │
└────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────┴────────────────────────────┘
```

The **newtype pattern** with tuple structs is very idiomatic. It gives you type safety for free:

```rust
struct Meters(f64);
struct Feet(f64);

fn run(distance: Meters) { println!("{} m", distance.0); } // .0 = first field

run(Meters(5.0));    // ✅
// run(Feet(5.0));   // ❌ different types, even though both wrap f64
```

---

## 3. Adding behavior with `impl`

Methods and constructors go in an `impl` block:

```rust
struct Rectangle { width: f64, height: f64 }

impl Rectangle {
    // Associated function (no self): like a static method. `new` is just a convention.
    fn new(width: f64, height: f64) -> Self { Self { width, height } }
    fn square(size: f64) -> Self { Self::new(size, size) }

    fn area(&self) -> f64 { self.width * self.height }   // read-only borrow
    fn scale(&mut self, k: f64) { self.width *= k; self.height *= k; } // mutable borrow
    fn into_dims(self) -> (f64, f64) { (self.width, self.height) }    // takes ownership
}
```

The type of the `self` receiver is the important part. It says what the method does to the instance:

```
  Receiver     Meaning                     After the call...        Python/C# analogy
  ─────────    ─────────────────────────   ──────────────────────   ─────────────────
  &self        borrow, read only           caller still owns it     normal getter
  &mut self    borrow, may modify          caller still owns it     setter / mutator
  self         take ownership (consume)    caller can't use it      (no equivalent)
  (none)       associated function         -                        @staticmethod / static
```

Using it:

```rust
let mut r = Rectangle::new(3.0, 4.0);   // `::` for associated functions
println!("{}", r.area());               // `.` for methods → 12
r.scale(2.0);
let (w, h) = r.into_dims();             // r is consumed here
// r.area();                            // ❌ use after move
```

Rust adds `&` and `&mut` for you automatically when you call methods (*auto-referencing*). That's why you write `r.area()` and not `(&r).area()`.

You can also have **several `impl` blocks** for one struct. That's handy for grouping related functionality.

---

## 4. Getting free behavior with `#[derive]`

A struct can't be printed, compared, or cloned until it implements the matching traits. For common traits, the compiler can write the code for you:

```rust
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]
struct Point { x: i32, y: i32 }

let p = Point { x: 1, y: 2 };
println!("{:?}", p);    // Point { x: 1, y: 2 }
println!("{:#?}", p);   // pretty-printed over several lines
let q = p.clone();
assert_eq!(p, q);       // needs PartialEq
```

Common derives are `Debug`, `Clone`, `Copy` (only if every field is `Copy`), `PartialEq`/`Eq`, `Hash`, and `Default`. This is roughly like Python's `@dataclass` generating `__repr__` and `__eq__`.

---

## 5. Memory layout: where does a struct live?

A struct is stored **inline**, wherever you put it: on the stack, inside another struct, or inside a `Vec`. It is not automatically on the heap like a C# class object. Only fields that own heap data point to the heap:

```
  STACK (user1)                               HEAP
 ┌──────────────────────────────┐
 │ username: ptr ───────────────┼───────► "lightbridge"
 │           len = 11, cap = 11 │
 │ email:    ptr ───────────────┼───────► "lb@example.com"
 │           len = 14, cap = 14 │
 │ active:   true               │
 │ login_count: 0               │
 └──────────────────────────────┘
```

Note that the Rust compiler is free to **reorder fields** to reduce padding. If you need a C-compatible layout, for example for FFI, use `#[repr(C)]`.

On semantics: Rust structs act like C# **structs**, not classes. They are values, and assignment **moves** them (or copies them, if `Copy`). Shared references exist only through explicit borrows (`&`) or smart pointers (`Rc`, `Arc`).

---

## 6. Storing references inside a struct needs lifetimes

Owned fields like `String` are the simple default. If a struct holds a **reference**, you have to tell the compiler how long that reference must stay valid:

```rust
struct Excerpt<'a> {
    text: &'a str,   // "an Excerpt can't outlive the string it borrows"
}
```

A good rule while learning is to **use owned types in structs** (`String`, `Vec<T>`) until you have a clear reason to borrow.

---

## 7. Visibility and encapsulation

Privacy works at the **module** level, and it is private by default. A `pub` struct can still have private fields:

```rust
pub mod geometry {
    pub struct Circle { radius: f64 }          // field is private

    impl Circle {
        pub fn new(radius: f64) -> Option<Self> {
            if radius > 0.0 { Some(Self { radius }) } else { None }
        }
        pub fn radius(&self) -> f64 { self.radius }
    }
}
```

Code outside the `geometry` module **cannot** write `Circle { radius: -1.0 }`. It has to go through `new`, so the rule "radius > 0" is guaranteed by the type system. This is the "make invalid states unrepresentable" idea, and it fits well with the SOLID and clean-architecture style you prefer.

---

## Quick comparison with languages you know

```
┌──────────────┬──────────────────┬──────────────────┬──────────────────────┐
│              │ Rust struct      │ C# class         │ Python @dataclass    │
├──────────────┼──────────────────┼──────────────────┼──────────────────────┤
│ Semantics    │ value (move)     │ reference        │ reference            │
│ Null fields  │ impossible¹      │ possible         │ possible (None)      │
│ Constructor  │ convention (new) │ keyword          │ auto __init__        │
│ Inheritance  │ none             │ yes              │ yes                  │
│ Interfaces   │ traits           │ interface        │ Protocol / ABC       │
│ Mutability   │ per binding      │ per field        │ per field (frozen=)  │
└──────────────┴──────────────────┴──────────────────┴──────────────────────┘
 ¹ "Maybe absent" is written explicitly as Option<T>
```

---

### Key takeaways
1. A `struct` holds **data**, `impl` holds **behavior**, and traits provide **shared behavior** (polymorphism).
2. Mutability belongs to the **binding**, not to individual fields.
3. The receiver (`&self`, `&mut self`, `self`) tells you how each method treats ownership.
4. Structs are **values**: they move by default, and you opt into `Clone`/`Copy`.
5. Private fields plus a `new` constructor give you strong encapsulation.
